title: Why a Korean Night Out Comes in Numbered Rounds

slides.kicker: IT ISN'T ONE DINNER. IT'S THREE PLACES.
slides.headline: A Korean night out is **numbered** — and dinner is only round one.
slides.note: Nobody asks if you want another drink. They ask whether you're going to the second round.

slides.headline: It has a name: **chasu**
slides.body: Chasu (차수) means the count of rounds. 1-cha, 2-cha, 3-cha. The question is never 'one more drink?' — it's 'are you in for 2-cha?'

slides.headline: Each round is a **different building**
slides.body: 1-cha is dinner, usually grilled pork and soju. 2-cha moves to a beer place or a tent bar. 3-cha is a karaoke room.

slides.headline: Moving is **the whole point**
slides.body: The walk between places resets the table. New seats, new mix of people talking. Staying in one bar all night is what feels strange here.

slides.headline: At work it had **its own rules**
slides.body: For a hoesik (회식), the company dinner, the boss decided how far the night went. Skipping 1-cha read as skipping the team.

slides.headline: Nobody pours **their own drink**
slides.body: You fill the glass next to you, they fill yours. Two hands for someone older. The habit is what keeps a table checking on each other.

slides.headline: Here's what **outsiders miss**
slides.body: In most countries a night out is one bar you settle into. In Korea it's a route through a neighbourhood, and everyone knows the stops.

slides.headline: new karaoke rooms are **coin rooms**
slides.body: Coin noraebang take payment by the song, sell no alcohol, and made up over 70% of the karaoke rooms that opened last year.

slides.headline: So 3-cha **split in two**
slides.body: Office teams stop at 1-cha or make 2-cha a coffee shop. Younger crowds go to a coin room instead — often sober, sometimes alone.

slides.headline: Korea, explained **by a Korean.**
slides.body: Follow for the context behind the things Korea does.

caption:
A Korean night out doesn't run on drinking more, it runs on moving. Dinner is 1-cha. Beer somewhere else is 2-cha. A karaoke room is 3-cha, and each one is a different building.

What outsiders read as heavy drinking is mostly relocation. Every move resets the table — new seats, new conversations, and a natural exit for anyone who wants one.

The third round didn't die, it split. Office teams stop earlier or make 2-cha a coffee shop, while younger crowds go to a coin karaoke room that charges by the song and serves no alcohol. Over 70% of the karaoke rooms opening now are that kind.
reply:
The detail that catches people out: 1-cha is where the real conversation happens, not 3-cha. By the karaoke room nobody is talking — they're taking turns with a microphone. If you only have one round in you, take the first one.

And there's a fourth stop the cards left off. Haejangguk (해장국), hangover soup, is a whole restaurant category that opens early for exactly this reason.

How does a night out work where you live — one place, or a route?

I post one of these every morning, Korea explained by a Korean who lives here. Follow @whatshotkorea so you catch the next one.
fact_check: 'Over 70% of newly opened karaoke rooms were coin noraebang last year': 한국경제 1 Nov 2024, citing the karaoke industry association. The same piece reports 243 new karaoke businesses in the first nine months of 2024 against 510 in all of 2023, and closures outnumbering openings for eight straight years. The card says 'last year' rather than a date because the figure is the association's annual share, so re-check which year applies before publishing.

The total count is falling while the coin share rises — those are two different facts and the cards keep them apart. Earlier drafts used the raw count (27,779 in Nov 2021, down from a 2011 peak near 35,300, per 서울경제 28 Jul 2019 and later reporting) to claim the third round was disappearing. That framing was wrong: the room is not vanishing, it is changing type. Do not put it back.

Coin noraebang charge per song and are not licensed to serve alcohol, which is why the card can say they sit outside the drinking round. That is a structural fact about the format, not a survey result.

The age split — office teams stopping earlier, younger crowds in coin rooms — is written with no numbers on purpose. No age-broken-down statistic was found for coin noraebang use, so the slide describes the pattern and claims no share. Do not add a percentage here without a primary source.

The 52-hour workweek took effect for large companies on 1 July 2018 and was phased in for smaller ones afterwards. The slide says only that nights got shorter 'since the 52-hour week', which holds regardless of the phase-in date, but do not add a date to the card without checking the phase that applies.

The link between the 52-hour week and shorter drinking rounds is what Korean press reported alongside the noraebang decline, including the line that 2-cha moved to coffee shops. It is press framing, not a controlled study, so the card keeps it as an observation about teams rather than a proven cause.
Pouring etiquette — filling someone else's glass, two hands for a senior — is common practice, not a rule anyone enforces. Written as a habit for that reason.

Hoesik attendance: describing it as effectively expected is fair for the culture the cards describe, but it is not a legal or written obligation. The slide says it 'read as skipping the team', which is about perception, not policy. Keep it that way.
1-cha as grilled pork and soju is the common case, not a fixed menu. The slide says 'usually'.
Haejangguk in the reply is described as a restaurant category that opens early, which is accurate; no claim is made about hangover cure efficacy.
